what_it_does: Processing a one-million-word prompt through a large language model requires so much memory and computation that no single GPU can handle it; the KV cache (the model's growing record of every word it has seen) alone is enormous, and the attention step — where every new word looks back at every previous word — has cost that grows quadratically with length. This paper describes how Meta's inference system splits long sequences across many GPUs using a ring of communicating machines, achieving near-linear speedup and processing a 1-million-token prompt in 77 seconds across 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Split the input sequence into chunks and give each chunk to a different GPU. Each GPU then runs the attention step only on its local chunk, but needs to see the key and value vectors (the running notes about past words) from every other GPU. You solve that by circulating information around a ring of GPUs.

How it works. Each GPU holds a contiguous chunk of the sequence. In the pass-KV variant, the key/value vectors travel one hop per step around a ring of GPUs; each GPU computes partial attention between its fixed query chunk and the visiting key/value chunk, then passes the key/value chunk to the next neighbor — overlapping that communication with computation. In pass-Q, the query vectors travel instead while key/value vectors stay fixed; at the end, partial results are gathered back to each query's home GPU. Which variant is used depends on a simple ratio: if the fraction of new tokens relative to total cached tokens exceeds a threshold (roughly 12.5% for the Llama 3 405B model), pass-KV wins because it sends less data; when the cache is mostly from prior turns and only a few new tokens arrive, pass-Q wins.

The key design choice. Load balancing is subtle with causal attention (where token N only looks back at tokens 1 through N). Naively, GPUs holding later tokens do far more work. The fix is to cut each sequence into 2N chunks for N GPUs and pair chunk i with chunk 2N-i-1 on the same GPU, so every GPU gets one early (light) and one late (heavy) chunk that together take equal time.

The result. On 16 nodes (128 H100 GPUs), a 1-million-token Llama 3 405B prefill finishes in 77 seconds at 93% parallelization efficiency and 63% of theoretical peak compute, versus roughly 1200 seconds on a single 8-GPU node.
